attrs.description: The four-dimensional continuum combining the three dimensions of space with one dimension of time, whose geometry is dynamical in general relativity.
A state of strongly interacting matter in which quarks and gluons are not confined inside hadrons.
The compact, positively charged core of an atom containing protons and neutrons.
A vector that lives in the tangent space at a single point of a manifold, representing an instantaneous direction and rate of change at that point.
A measure of how much a manifold deviates from being flat, captured by how a vector changes when parallel-transported around a closed loop.
The stress-energy tensor: a description of the density and flux of energy and momentum in spacetime, acting as the source of gravity.
A current describing the transport of particles or conserved charge through the fluid.
Hydrodynamic fields describing departures from local equilibrium, including viscous stresses and diffusion currents.
The dissipative transport of conserved charge caused by spatial gradients and interactions.
The relativistic velocity field tangent to the fluid worldlines.
The scalar expansion of a fluid congruence, describing the local rate at which neighboring fluid elements separate.
The time required for half of the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay.
The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus.
A helium-4 nucleus consisting of two protons and two neutrons.
The bending of light from a distant source as it passes near a massive object, caused by the curvature of spacetime around that mass.
Radioactive decay in which an unstable nucleus emits an alpha particle.
The classical model in which gravity is treated as an instantaneous attractive force between masses, recovered from general relativity as a low-velocity, weak-field approximation.
The theory of spacetime and motion in inertial frames when gravity is neglected.
The regime where gravitational fields are weak and velocities are much smaller than the speed of light, so spacetime curvature can be treated as a small perturbation on flat space.
The requirement that physical laws take the same form in all inertial frames related by Lorentz transformations.
The large-sample condition under which radioactive decay is well described statistically.
The study of vector spaces and the linear maps between them: vectors, matrices, bases, eigenvalues, and linear transformations.
An abstract set of objects (vectors) that can be added together and scaled by numbers, satisfying a fixed set of axioms.
The study of curves, surfaces, and manifolds using calculus and linear algebra — the mathematical language used to describe curved spacetime.
The vector space of all possible tangent vectors at a single point of a manifold — the local 'flat' approximation of the manifold at that point.
A microscopic description of matter in terms of distribution functions and particle interactions.
Changes between coordinate descriptions used to express physical quantities without changing the underlying physics.
Exponential functions used to model continuous growth or decay processes.
Relate the curvature of spacetime directly to the energy and momentum of whatever matter and radiation are present, forming the core field equation of general relativity.
conditions: Valid in any smooth Lorentzian spacetime manifold
Assumes a classical (non-quantum) description of matter and gravity
representations: Component form for a specific metric, e.g. Schwarzschild or FLRW

attrs.description: Equations expressing local conservation of energy-momentum and particle or charge currents.
Causal and stable relativistic dissipative hydrodynamic equations.
An equation describing the exponential decrease of the number of undecayed nuclei over time.
A rule for moving a vector along a curve on a manifold while keeping it 'as parallel as possible' to itself at each step.
A continuum description of relativistic fluids that includes dissipative effects such as viscosity.
A moment expansion that approximates a kinetic distribution function using a finite set of macroscopic moments.
Projection of a tensor or vector onto the subspace orthogonal to the fluid four-velocity.
Solar eclipse expeditions led by Arthur Eddington that measured the deflection of starlight by the Sun, providing early observational support for general relativity.
The Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider, used to study matter under extreme temperatures and densities.

nodes.label: Intro to the Einstein Field Equations (sample resource)
Misconception: gravity is a pulling force

attrs.description: The idea that gravity is a force pulling objects directly toward one another through space, rather than the effect of objects following straight paths (geodesics) through curved spacetime.
Non-luminous matter inferred from its gravitational effects, making up most of the matter in the universe.
Bosonic matter which behaves like a wave on sub-galactic scales due to coherence of wave functions at cold temperatures with a small mass.
Particles with integer spin; they obey Bose–Einstein statistics, so any number of them can occupy the same quantum state.
Bose–Einstein condensate: a state in which a large fraction of bosons occupy the same lowest-energy quantum state and behave as one coherent matter wave.
The superposition of waves, producing a pattern of reinforcement where they are in phase and cancellation where they are out of phase.
The growth of galaxies, clusters and the cosmic web from small initial density fluctuations through gravitational instability.
Surfaces where rays or particle streams cross and focus, producing sharp peaks in intensity or density.
A first-order Lagrangian model of structure formation in which particles move on straight lines from their initial positions, displaced along the gradient of the initial gravitational potential.
Describes the phase-space evolution of a particle gas.
